catalog_quote: Baima is a tone language with a complex interrelation between (a) pitch height, (b) voice quality of the vowel, and (c) vowel length. Baima has three contrastive tones, which in a prepausal position all end in a falling pitch contour. ... Baima morphemes (lexical and grammatical) are generally monosyllabic, but words are generally disyllabic. Polysyllabic words are mostly composite, formed through compounding. Content morphemes in Baima are specified for lexical tone ... In connected speech, grammatical morphemes are prosodically weak, they usually have shorter duration than content morphemes and no fixed tone value ... In polysyllabic words, each syllable bears its own (etymological) tone (correlated with a specific phonation type). audit.reasoning: The deciding quotation is verbatim in the held HAL author manuscript of Chirkova, Kocjančič Antolík & Amelot 2023 (JIPA Illustration) at the stated pages (ms 39, 44-45). The source is a 2023 instrumental description by the language's main specialist, newer than and citing every grammar/sketch in Glottolog's list; it states three lexical tones, per-syllable etymological tone in polysyllables and compounds, prosodically weak toneless grammatical morphemes, and prominence only at the phrasal (focus) level, which is exactly the catalog's 'tonal, no word-stress rule, domain PHRASE' coding. The one additional open prosody paper (Chirkova, Language and Linguistics, HAL hal-04201418) was fetched sources to and is silent on stress while confirming the three-tone system. sources.quote: 'the three contrastive tonal categories in Baima have likely arisen through an overlay of the phonation difference in consonants ... and the phonation difference in vowels (tense vs. lax, with pitch and vowel duration as co-articulated cues)'. No statement on word-level stress anywhere in the 35-pp paper.
